In his monograph on this process, Michael Dummett published three proofs of the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem and proposed a variation on the Borda count, which remains vulnerable to the "tactical" form of this action. In Old English, this concept is not distinguished in the dative singular and plural. Agreement with non-human plurals in Arabic will correspond to one of these frequently marked by the suffix "at". A 1997 Fareed Zakaria essay in Foreign Affairs warns of the rise of illiberal types of this system. Anatol Rapoport created a simulation of this concept using four lines of BASIC code, while another simulation is called Pavlov. In that work, she contrasted female American adolescents with their sexually active counterparts in Polynesia. One measure of the power of this structure is price minus marginal cost all over price, called the Lerner Index. One section of this work describes how the working poor have a mental torpor that make them incapable of "rational conversation," "tender sentiment," or "just judgment." A paper titled "[this concept]: Knowns and Unknowns" described advances made by the Abecedarian Project. The amount of this phenomenon in industry contexts may be measured by the Grubel–Lloyd index. Increasing returns to scale in this phenomenon produce the home-market effect. This activity's "professionalization" is examined in the most widely cited book by professionalism theorist Eliot Freidson. An analogy to this human activity is used in the title of a 1969 paper questioning Australia's doctrine of terra nullius by Rhys Jones. Alfred Blumstein's focus on cases in which this phenomenon is constant with age was contested by Travis Hirschi and Michael Gottfredson. "Herbert and Eve Clark found that even though young children frequently made the sound represented by this letter while babbling, it was one of the last they learned in actual speech.
